Thank you for your interest in contributing to our Accessibility Hub! Our mission is to create the most reliable, well-organized, and user-friendly resource for anyone involved in making the world more accessible. This includes tools, guidelines, and resources for improving digital accessibility in areas such as screen readers, assistive technologies, visual impairments, and more. By contributing, you help developers, individuals with disabilities, accessibility testers, educators, and advocates find the resources they need to support accessible technology.

Promote Awareness: Provide actionable and relatable accessibility information. Serve All Skill Levels: Create resources for beginners, experienced professionals, educators, and end users. Cover Diverse Topics: Include tools, best practices, regulations, user experience insights, and accessibility technologies. Improve Accessibility Culture: Reduce barriers and make digital spaces inclusive.

Headings (H1–H6), nav labels, and primary link labels must be plain text; do not include emoji characters. Decorative emojis may be used in body text sparingly and must not be the sole carrier of meaning. Always provide clear text. Generated artifacts (e.g., Mermaid maps, legends): emojis are stripped from node labels; legends provide textual explanations. Authoring rules: Replace heading emojis with text-only headings. If you keep emojis in body text, prefer 🙂 with adjacent visible text. In MDX, wrap directly; in MD, rely on our build tooling. UI components: Homepage cards render as: title + {emoji}; the span is only rendered when an emoji is present. Tooling and CI: Our Docusaurus build uses a remark plugin that strips emojis from headings. Remark lint runs in CI and will fail PRs that include emojis in headings.
Not sure where to start? Here’s how you can pitch in:
Check the last section in the sidebar called Contribute. Here you'll find examples of resources we need, as well as requests for improvements to existing materials.

Have your own idea? Follow these steps: Browse /docs/ to find the right folder for your topic. Copy the /docs/.template.md file as a starting point for your new resource. Rename your file (e.g., screen-readers.md, dos-and-donts.md). ⚠️ Do not name files intro.md or index.md — these are reserved for folder landing pages.

At the top of every Markdown file, include your frontmatter to classify, tag, and describe the resource. Frontmatter is essential YAML metadata included in every resource file to ensure classification, seamless system integration, and proper organization. Here are the key highlights: Purpose: Frontmatter provides structure by categorizing and describing resources, making them easier to manage and access. Required Fields: title: A concise, descriptive name for the resource (e.g., "Introduction to ARIA"). type: The content type (e.g., overview, guide, tutorial, reference). level: The intended audience expertise level (beginner, intermediate, or advanced). status: The development stage of the resource (draft, wip, published). topics: Tags summarizing the content, with a focus on: Broad categories like accessibility. Specific prefixes such as assistive-technology. More about topics here the Topics guide For the full guide, refer to FRONTMATTER_GUIDE.
Create a Pull Request (PR) in our GitHub repository. Include a summary of your changes, why they're important, and mention any related GitHub issues.
Each directory in /docs/ can have an intro.md as a topic landing page.

Keep it short and clear (max 2–3 paragraphs). Define the purpose of the section and direct users to subtopics. Mention the expected audience, whether beginners, experienced developers, end-users, or educators. Ensure the section remains partially visible above visual diagrams or flatmaps on the site.

When submitting a PR, ensure: All required frontmatter fields are present. Optional fields are only added if relevant (e.g., eta for planned work). Files are placed in the correct folder within /docs/. Your content aligns with our accessibility-first values. Our automated PR checks will validate: Proper metadata format and values. Required fields like title, type, level, and topics. For planned or in-progress resources: an eta field (completion date) must be included. ⚠️ Tip: If there’s an issue or discussion related to your PR, reference it in the description!
To maintain consistency, use the following topics when tagging your content:
accessibility assistive-technology visual-impairment design-principles standards (WCAG, ARIA, etc.)
tool:JAWS tool:NVDA tool:VoiceOver tool:Narrator tool:Orca

provider:freedom-scientific provider:microsoft provider:apple provider:nv-access Include your tags as specific and accurate as possible — these improve searchability and structure for other contributors. For more details, check out the Topics by Category.

Focus on Accessibility: Write with an accessibility-first mindset, including inclusive examples (e.g., using headings, lists, and descriptive text). Use Clear Language: Avoid technical jargon whenever possible. Cater to all skill levels. Cite Reliable Sources: Reference official accessibility standards (e.g., WCAG, ARIA specifications). Test Recommendations: Ensure tools or techniques described in your resource are tested and validated.
Contributors help ensure this hub is valuable and up-to-date by: Responding to resource requests. Keeping planned content on schedule (eta informed). Updating draft or wip resources once complete.

If your resource is still being developed, set its status to planned or wip and include an estimated completion date (eta). Why?: It prevents duplication. Maintainers and other contributors can monitor progress or assist. Thank you for helping make the Accessibility Hub a trusted, inclusive, and insightful resource!

Accessibility in software is often associated with user interfaces, but it is equally important in API and schema design. Accessible APIs improve usability for developers using assistive technologies, enhance code readability, and support better tooling integration. This guide outlines key strategies Java developers can adopt to make their APIs more inclusive.

If you only have 10 minutes, do this: Use clear, pronounceable identifiers. See: 1. Use Clear Word Separators Avoid abbreviations that confuse AT. See: 2. Avoid Abbreviations Prefer structured content over HTML blobs. See: 8. Deliver Structured Content, Not HTML Blobs Include media accessibility metadata. See: 10. Provide Metadata for Media Make docs accessible and include examples. See: 11. Make API Documentation Accessible Add CI checks for required accessibility fields. See: 13. Integrate Accessibility Testing into CI/CD

Screen readers rely on word boundaries to interpret identifiers. Without separators, compound words become opaque and hard to parse. Clear separators also improve parsing by code generators and linters. Why this matters (refs): RFC 3986 recommends readable, hierarchical URIs; clear tokens aid comprehension and tooling. UUID format is defined in RFC 4122. RFC 3986 (URIs): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986 RFC 4122 (UUIDs): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4122
data_base64 dataContentType data-content-type com.example.api /api/v1/resource 123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000
datacontenttype

Abbreviations can confuse screen readers and increase cognitive load for users. Prefer full words or expand on first use. When abbreviations are necessary, provide an expansion in documentation. Why this matters (ref): WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.1.4 (Abbreviations) recommends providing expansions or definitions for abbreviations. WCAG 2.2 Quick Ref: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#abbreviations
privateKey accessToken userProfile
pvtKey accTkn usrProf
Some characters are visually ambiguous and can be misinterpreted by humans and machines alike.
O vs 0 1 vs l vs I Avoid using these characters in isolation or in critical identifiers like URIs, keys, or codes.

Accessible APIs are well-documented. Ensure: Descriptions are complete and avoid jargon. Examples use accessible naming. Error messages are descriptive and avoid cryptic codes. Use tools like Swagger/OpenAPI with annotations that support accessibility, such as @Schema(description = "...") in Springdoc.

Accessible naming conventions improve compatibility with: Code generators Static analysis tools Documentation generators Assistive technologies For example, using dataContentType allows Java tools to generate getDataContentType() methods, which are easier to read and use.

Use screen readers like NVDA, JAWS, or VoiceOver to test how your API documentation and schema are interpreted. This helps identify issues that may not be obvious during development. Official resources: NVDA: https://www.nvaccess.org/ JAWS (Freedom Scientific): https://www.freedomscientific.com/products/software/jaws/ VoiceOver (Apple): https://support.apple.com/guide/voiceover/welcome/mac

Accessibility should be part of the data model, not just the front-end. Provide text alternatives and descriptive fields where media or complex UI will be rendered. Why this matters (ref): WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.1.1 (Non-text Content) requires text alternatives for non-text content (e.g., images). WCAG 2.2 Quick Ref — 1.1.1: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#non-text-content
{ "imageUrl": "https://example.com/image.jpg", "altText": "A person using a wheelchair entering a building" }

Avoid sending pre-formatted HTML in API responses. Use structured JSON to describe content hierarchy. This preserves information and relationships so UIs can render them accessibly. Why this matters (refs): WCAG 2.2 — 1.3.1 Info and Relationships: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#info-and-relationships JSON Schema (describe structure/constraints): https://json-schema.org/ OpenAPI Specification (document your API): https://spec.openapis.org/oas/latest.html
documents.s: 8. Deliver Structured Content, Not HTML Blobs

documents.t: { "content": [ { "type": "heading", "level": 2, "text": "Our Mission" }, { "type": "paragraph", "text": "We aim to do great things." } ] }

For interactive components like tabs or accordions, provide structural metadata that allows UI layers to apply appropriate ARIA roles and attributes. Why this matters (refs): WAI-ARIA 1.2 (roles, states, properties): https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/ ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) patterns: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/
documents.s: 9. Provide Structural Metadata to Support ARIA in UIs

documents.t: { "tabs": [ { "id": "tab1", "label": "Overview", "panelId": "panel1", "isSelected": true } ] }

Ensure media resources include accessibility metadata such as captions, transcripts, audio descriptions, and descriptions for images. Why this matters (refs): WCAG 2.2 — 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded): https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#captions-prerecorded WCAG 2.2 — 1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#audio-description-or-media-alternative-prerecorded WebVTT (W3C): https://www.w3.org/TR/webvtt/

{ "featuredVideo": { "videoUrl": "https://example.com/video.mp4", "captionFileUrl": "https://example.com/captions.vtt", "transcriptUrl": "https://example.com/transcript.txt", "description": "Demo of our product features." } }

Use semantic HTML with proper heading structure. Ensure keyboard navigation and color contrast. Include accessible examples and explain accessibility-specific fields. Create a dedicated Accessibility section in your API docs. References: WCAG 2.2 Overview/Quick Ref: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/ WAI: Planning and Managing Accessibility: https://www.w3.org/WAI/planning-and-managing/

Error messages should be structured, human-readable, and helpful. Prefer standardized formats like Problem Details for HTTP APIs (RFC 7807) so tools and assistive technologies can present consistent information. Reference: RFC 7807 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7807

{ "type": "https://example.com/problems/user-already-exists", "title": "User already exists", "status": 409, "detail": "This email address is already registered. Please try logging in or use a different email address.", "instance": "/signup/requests/12345", "errors": [ { "field": "emailAddress", "message": "Email is already registered" } ] }

Automate checks for accessibility-related fields and formats using API and schema testing tools. Ideas and tools: Spectral (OpenAPI linting): https://meta.stoplight.io/docs/spectral/ Schemathesis (property-based testing for APIs): https://schemathesis.readthedocs.io/ OpenAPI Validator (OpenAPI Initiative): https://www.openapis.org/resources/tools
Validate presence of altText, captionFileUrl, transcriptUrl Ensure structured content format (e.g., JSON Schema validation) Confirm clarity of error messages (e.g., RFC 7807 Problem Details)

Contract testing ensures that the interaction between a consumer (e.g., a frontend app) and a provider (e.g., an API) adheres to a shared agreement, or contract. This is especially useful in microservices architectures and can be extended to include accessibility metadata in API responses. By defining accessibility-related fields (like altText, captionFileUrl, transcriptUrl, etc.) in your contract, you ensure that both the backend and frontend teams are aligned on what accessibility data must be present and how it should be structured Use tools like Pact or Spring Cloud Contract to validate presence and format of accessibility metadata.

Spring Cloud Contract is a powerful tool for JVM-based applications that supports Consumer-Driven Contracts (CDC). It allows you to define contracts in Groovy or YAML and automatically generates tests for both producers and consumers. Spring Cloud Contract Overview - https://spring.io/projects/spring-cloud-contract Baeldung Tutorial on Spring Cloud Contract - https://www.baeldung.com/spring-cloud-contract Official Documentation - https://docs.spring.io/spring-cloud-contract/docs/current/reference/html/using.html

Pact is a language-agnostic contract testing tool that supports HTTP and message-based interactions. It’s widely used in microservices environments and supports multiple languages including Java, JavaScript, and Python. Pact Documentation - https://docs.pact.io/ Baeldung Guide to Pact2 - https://www.baeldung.com/pact-junit-consumer-driven-contracts Example: Pact (Java, HTTP)​ A consumer test can assert that accessibility fields are present and correctly typed. @Pact(consumer = "webapp") public RequestResponsePact getImage(PactDslWithProvider builder) { return builder .given("image exists with accessibility metadata") .uponReceiving("get image metadata") .path("/api/images/42") .method("GET") .willRespondWith() .status(200) .headers(Map.of("Content-Type", "application/json")) .body(newJsonBody(o -> { o.stringType("imageUrl", "https://example.com/image.jpg"); o.stringMatcher("altText", ".+", "A person using a wheelchair entering a building"); o.stringType("captionFileUrl", "https://example.com/captions.vtt"); o.stringType("transcriptUrl", "https://example.com/transcript.txt"); }).build()) .toPact(); } Example: Spring Cloud Contract (Groovy DSL)​ Producer-side contract requiring accessibility fields in the response. org.springframework.cloud.contract.spec.Contract.make { description "Get video with captions and transcript" request { method GET() url "/api/videos/123" } response { status OK() headers { contentType(applicationJson()) } body( featuredVideo: [ videoUrl: 'https://example.com/video.mp4', captionFileUrl: 'https://example.com/captions.vtt', transcriptUrl: 'https://example.com/transcript.txt', description: 'Demo of our product features.' ] ) bodyMatchers { jsonPath('$.featuredVideo.captionFileUrl', byRegex('.+\\.vtt')) jsonPath('$.featuredVideo.transcriptUrl', byRegex('.+')) jsonPath('$.featuredVideo.description', byRegex('.+')) } } }
Automated checks confirm presence, not quality. Establish a lightweight review process so humans validate that accessibility data is accurate, complete, and useful.

Alt text (images/icons): Is it accurate, concise, and non-redundant? Avoid “image of…”. Don’t describe purely decorative images; use empty alt instead. Captions and transcripts (audio/video): Are captions synchronized and accurate? Do transcripts include speaker changes and important non-speech info? Provide audio description or a media alternative when needed. Labels, help text, and headings: Are field/parameter names and descriptions clear, unambiguous, and consistent? Do headings communicate structure? Error copy: Is guidance actionable and free of jargon? Does it identify the field and the fix?

Images have meaningful altText or are explicitly marked decorative. (WCAG 2.2 — 1.1.1) Time-based media include captions and a transcript; audio description or equivalent is available where required. (WCAG 2.2 — 1.2.x) Headings/sections in docs follow a logical outline. (WCAG 2.2 — 2.4.6) Form fields and parameters have clear labels or instructions. (WCAG 2.2 — 3.3.2)

WCAG 2.2 — 1.1.1 Non-text Content: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#non-text-content WAI Images Tutorial: https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/ WAI Alt Text Decision Tree: https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/decision-tree/ WCAG 2.2 — 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded): https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#captions-prerecorded WCAG 2.2 — 1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#audio-description-or-media-alternative-prerecorded WCAG 2.2 — 2.4.6 Headings and Labels: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#headings-and-labels WCAG 2.2 — 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#labels-or-instructions Plain language guidance (US): https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/
If required accessibility data is missing or a consumer cannot support a rich experience, degrade gracefully so users aren’t blocked.

Provide explicit nullability and semantics: Distinguish missing vs. decorative (e.g., altText: null vs altText: "" with isDecorative: true). Document expectations in OpenAPI. Prefer omission over broken experiences: If a video lacks captions/transcript, supply a transcript placeholder and set a flag isAccessible:false, or omit the video and return a clear Problem Details error explaining the deficiency (RFC 7807). Content negotiation: Offer text-only or simplified variants (e.g., Accept: application/vnd.example.article+json; profile=text-only). Defaults for structure: When structural metadata is absent, return plain, semantic content instead of ARIA-dependent structures. Log and monitor: Emit structured logs/metrics when accessibility contracts are not met to prompt remediation.

Images: Use alt="" for decorative images; don’t invent misleading alt text. If a critical image has no alt, replace with an equivalent text message or link to description instead of showing an inaccessible element. Media: If captions/transcript are missing, do not autoplay; provide transcript link or disable playback behind an explanation. Widgets: If required roles/relationships are missing, render a native, semantic fallback rather than a broken custom control. Remember: “No ARIA is better than bad ARIA.”

WCAG 2.2 — 1.1.1 Non-text Content: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#non-text-content WCAG 2.2 — 1.2.x Time-based Media: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#time-based-media HTML Standard — img alt attribute: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/images.html#alt WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/ WAI — “No ARIA is better than bad ARIA”: https://www.w3.org/TR/using-aria/#no_aria_better_bad_aria RFC 7807 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7807
Accessibility succeeds when product, design, engineering, QA, and docs share a contract and workflow.

Define responsibilities: Use W3C’s Accessibility Roles and Responsibilities Mapping (ARRM) to assign who writes alt text, who validates captions, who owns schema fields, etc. Definition of Done: Add concrete a11y acceptance criteria (e.g., caption files present for all new videos; alt text reviewed; error messages follow RFC 7807) to stories and PR templates. Shared artifacts: Keep an “Accessibility” section in the API spec (OpenAPI) and in product docs describing required fields, examples, and contracts. Joint rituals: Run design reviews and contract testing sessions with both frontend and backend to verify accessibility metadata. Training/enablement: Provide periodic training on WCAG and AT usage for engineers, PMs, and tech writers.

W3C — Accessibility Roles and Responsibilities Mapping (ARRM): https://www.w3.org/WAI/roles/ WAI — Planning and Managing Accessibility: https://www.w3.org/WAI/planning-and-managing/ WAI — Curricula on Web Accessibility: https://www.w3.org/WAI/curricula/ W3C — ACT Rules (testing methodology): https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/ WCAG 2.2 Quick Ref: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/ The A11Y Project Checklist: https://www.a11yproject.com/checklist/

Repo: a11y-ai-readiness · Live results dashboard: view the live results Came here from the talk? What to do next has six steps you can start with tomorrow. A Spring Boot web app that serves one flow — register for a workshop — from two sets of templates. Same controller, same validation, same stylesheet, same data. Only the markup differs. The session list is asserted pixel-identical by a test; the registration form, where the testing happened, looks and behaves the same to a sighted mouse user. That one difference decides whether a screen reader user or an AI agent can complete the task at all.
documents.s: AI Agents Read Your Accessibility Tree, Not Your HTML

documents.t: Your UI has two consumers you probably don't test: assistive technology, and software acting on a user's behalf. Neither reads your HTML or your CSS. Both read the accessibility tree the browser builds from your markup — roles, names, states. An agent driving a browser asks that tree "what's on this page, and what can I do to it?" A screen reader asks the identical question. So a <div onclick> that looks like a button isn't a styling choice — it's a control that neither one can find. There is no separate "make it AI-ready" project. It's the same work, and it's already in your backlog as an accessibility ticket.

Three independent consumers, same task, both variants: Who tried it /accessible /inaccessible NVDA (screen reader, keyboard only) Completed Failed AI agent — Grok (grok-4.6) Completed Failed AI agent — Claude (claude-sonnet-5) Completed Failed Two unrelated vendors' models, tested separately, so this isn't one model's quirk. Agent runs — 5 runs per variant per provider, medians: Provider Variant Success Tool calls Tokens Cost/run Grok grok-4.6 /accessible 100% 11 36k $0.071 Grok grok-4.6 /inaccessible 0% 33 127k $0.247 Claude claude-sonnet-5 /accessible 100% 11 47k $0.104 Claude claude-sonnet-5 /inaccessible 0% 3 11k $0.027 Note the two shapes of failure. Grok kept hunting — 3× the calls, 3.5× the tokens, 3.5× the cost, and still no confirmation code. Claude recognised there was no reachable control and gave up after three calls. Cheap is not good news here: the transaction is lost either way. If that flow were a checkout, a booking, or a claim submission, an inaccessible UI is one your customer's agent cannot buy from. The agent perceives the page only through accessibility-tree primitives — Playwright's ariaSnapshot() to look, role/name lookups to act. Nothing in its toolset reads raw HTML or CSS, which is what makes the comparison meaningful. Screen reader (NVDA, keyboard only): on /accessible, 61 keystrokes to a confirmation code, with the validation error announced immediately. On /inaccessible the task couldn't be started: after the filter box, Tab leaves the page entirely — the filter box is the only reachable control. With a mouse, the meal-preference dropdown still could not be operated, and nothing was ever announced to explain why submission kept failing.

axe-core runs against both pages in the test suite: Page Violations Rules /accessible sessions & register 0 — /inaccessible sessions 4 (9 nodes) image-alt, landmark-one-main, page-has-heading-one, region /inaccessible register 4 (9 nodes) label, landmark-one-main, page-has-heading-one, region Run as a Lighthouse audit in Edge DevTools, the broken register form still scores 91/100 for accessibility. Those four findings are largely not the four defects that actually broke every consumer. A scanner can only flag code that at least tries to be a button, field, or link; code that never tries — the fake <div> dropdown — is invisible to it. A high score is not a tested page. Keep the scanner in CI, but it is a floor, not a verdict.

documents.t: You don't need a big project to start. What to Do Next walks you through six short steps on one flow of your own app: look at the accessibility tree, use only the keyboard, listen with a screen reader, find controls by role in your tests, keep a scanner in CI, and learn the WCAG rules behind each fix. To see which kind of test catches which defect, read Test What Scanners Miss.

Needs JDK 25 — nothing else. The Maven wrapper fetches its own Maven, and there is no Node/npm step. ./mvnw spring-boot:run Then open http://localhost:8080/, which links to both variants. Open DevTools' accessibility tree on each and compare — that is the whole demo in thirty seconds. The agent never runs during spring-boot:run or mvn test. To run it (needs xai.api.key / XAI_API_KEY or anthropic.api.key / ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, see secrets.properties.example): ./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.arguments="--agent.run=true --variant=accessible --provider=xai" Add --runs=5 to run both variants N times each in alternating A-B-B-A order and write a summary with medians and ranges. Each run writes a results/*.json with tool calls, tokens, estimated cost, and the action log. DashboardGeneratorTest regenerates results/dashboard.html from whatever is in results/ — no server or browser needed to view it.

documents.s: Case study 1: Same app, two markups — screen readers and AI agents

documents.t: Does inaccessible markup only hurt screen reader users, or does it also block AI agents that act for users in a browser?

One "register for a workshop" flow served from two sets of templates. Same controller, validation, CSS and data. Only the markup differs. To a sighted mouse user, the two versions look and work the same.

A screen reader user (NVDA, keyboard only) tried to register on both versions. Two AI agents from different vendors tried the same task, 5 runs per version each. The agents could only see the page through accessibility tree tools: Playwright's ariaSnapshot() to look, and role and name lookups to act. axe-core ran on both versions in the test suite, and Lighthouse ran in the browser.

Accessible version Inaccessible version Screen reader (NVDA) Completed Failed. The task couldn't even start. AI agent 1 Completed in all runs Failed in all runs. It used about 3× the tool calls and cost. AI agent 2 Completed in all runs Failed in all runs. It gave up after 3 calls. Lighthouse score — 91/100

Four markup defects: a <span onclick> instead of a link, placeholders instead of labels, a <div> pretending to be a dropdown, and an error shown only by color. The scanners flagged mostly other issues. The fake dropdown, the worst defect, was invisible to them.
Native HTML: <a href>, <label for>, <select>, and a role="alert" error message. Each fix maps to a WCAG rule, and each one unblocked the screen reader and the agents at the same time.

AI agents and screen readers read the same thing: the accessibility tree. One fix helps both. A high scanner score is not a tested page. See Test What Scanners Miss. A thin accessibility tree is also why end-to-end tests need brittle CSS selectors. Role-based locators fix both problems. A failing agent doesn't always cost more. One agent spent 3× more and failed; the other gave up cheaply and failed. Either way, the transaction was lost.

Have you fixed an accessibility problem, run an experiment, or tested a product with real users? Your story helps the next developer. Small fixes are welcome; they don't need to be big projects. Use this outline (about 300–800 words): ## Case study: <short title> **Author:** <name> · **Stack:** <languages, frameworks, tools> · **Link:** <repo or article, optional> ### The problem What was wrong, and who it affected. Which users or assistive technologies? ### How you found it User report, audit, scanner, manual test, screen reader test, usability session? ### What you changed Before and after code, if you can share it. Which WCAG rule does it relate to? ### How you checked the fix Which tests or users confirmed it works? ### Lessons for other developers Two to four points someone could apply tomorrow. A practical checklist based on WCAG 2.2 Level AA, the level most laws and contracts ask for. Each item shows the WCAG rule (success criterion) behind it, linked to the W3C page that explains it, and a quick way to check it. How to use it: run it on one user flow at a time, such as login or checkout, not the whole site at once. Items marked scanner are usually caught by axe, WAVE or Lighthouse. Everything else needs a person. Test What Scanners Miss explains why.

The accessibility tree is built from your HTML. Correct elements give screen readers and AI agents the right roles for free. Use semantic elements (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <footer>, <button>, <a href>) instead of styled <div>s. WCAG 1.3.1, 4.1.2. Check: open the browser's accessibility tree. Controls should show as button, link or textbox, not generic. One <h1>, then headings in order without skipping levels for styling. WCAG 1.3.1, 2.4.6. Check: list the headings with a browser extension or NVDA's Elements List (Insert+F7). They should read like a table of contents. Scanner: partly. Use lists (<ul>, <ol>, <dl>) for groups of items, such as navigation links. WCAG 1.3.1. Check: a screen reader should say "list, 5 items". Mark up page regions with landmarks, with exactly one <main>. WCAG 1.3.1, 2.4.1. Check: press D in NVDA to jump between landmarks. Scanner: yes. Give every page a unique, descriptive <title>. WCAG 2.4.2. Check: read the browser tab. It should say what the page is, for example "Register — Workshop 123". Set the page language with <html lang="en">. WCAG 3.1.1. Check: view source. Without it, screen readers may read the page in the wrong accent. Scanner: yes.

Many people never use a mouse: screen reader users, people with motor disabilities, power users and many AI agents. Every interactive element works with the keyboard alone. WCAG 2.1.1. Check: put the mouse away and complete the flow with Tab, Enter, Space, arrows and Esc. Focus order follows the reading order. WCAG 2.4.3. Check: Tab through the page. Avoid positive tabindex values, which break the natural order. Focus is always visible. Don't remove outline without replacing it. WCAG 2.4.7. Check: at every Tab stop you should see where you are. Focus is never hidden behind sticky headers, cookie banners or chat widgets. WCAG 2.4.11 (new in 2.2). Check: Tab through a long page with the sticky header visible. No keyboard traps. You can always Tab or Esc out of any component. WCAG 2.1.2. Check: Tab into embedded players, editors and date pickers, then try to leave. A "Skip to main content" link is the first thing in the Tab order on pages with long navigation. WCAG 2.4.1. Check: load the page and press Tab once.

Every control needs a role, a name and a state. Native HTML provides them. ARIA is for when native HTML can't. See ARIA Roles. Every control has an accessible name that matches its visible label. WCAG 4.1.2, 2.5.3. Check: icon-only buttons need aria-label; a button showing "Send" should not be named "Submit form". Scanner: partly. Use ARIA only when no native element exists, and never contradict the native role (for example <button role="link">). WCAG 4.1.2. Check: search the code for role=. Each one should have a reason. Scanner: catches invalid ARIA, not unnecessary ARIA. States are exposed and kept in sync: aria-expanded on toggles, aria-pressed on toggle buttons, aria-current="page" on the current nav link. WCAG 4.1.2. Check: open and close a menu while watching the accessibility tree. The state should change. Status messages are announced without moving focus: "Saved", "3 results", "Item added to cart". WCAG 4.1.3. Check: use role="status" (polite) or role="alert" (urgent), and listen with a screen reader. Link text makes sense on its own, or with its surrounding sentence. Avoid "click here" and "read more". WCAG 2.4.4. Check: open NVDA's Elements List, Links tab. Each link should be clear out of context.

Text contrast is at least 4.5:1 against its background. WCAG 1.4.3. Check: the color picker in Chrome or Firefox DevTools shows the ratio. Scanner: yes, except text on images. Large text has contrast of at least 3:1. Large means 24px, or 18.66px bold. WCAG 1.4.3. Controls, focus outlines and meaningful icons have contrast of at least 3:1. WCAG 1.4.11. Check: input borders and focus rings are the most common failures. Scanners don't check these. Color is never the only signal. Add text, an icon or a pattern. WCAG 1.4.1. Check: view the page in grayscale (DevTools → Rendering → Emulate vision deficiencies). Errors, required fields and chart lines should still be clear. Text can be resized to 200% without content being cut off. WCAG 1.4.4. Check: zoom the browser to 200%. Text spacing can be increased without breaking the layout. WCAG 1.4.12. Check: fixed-height containers with text are the usual cause. Use min-height instead.

Informative images have alt text that says what the image means, not what it looks like. WCAG 1.1.1. Check: a scanner finds missing alt; only a person can judge whether it's useful. Scanner: partly. Decorative images use alt="" so screen readers skip them. WCAG 1.1.1. Charts and diagrams have a text alternative: a summary, or the data as a table. WCAG 1.1.1. Videos have captions. WCAG 1.2.2. Check: review auto-generated captions; they often get names and technical terms wrong. Videos have audio description when important information is only shown visually. WCAG 1.2.5. Audio-only content has a transcript. WCAG 1.2.1. No auto-playing sound, and moving content (carousels, animations) can be paused. WCAG 1.4.2, 2.2.2.

Forms are where most user flows fail, for people and for agents. Every field has a visible <label> connected with for and id. A placeholder is not a label: it disappears when you type. WCAG 3.3.2, 1.3.1. Check: click the label text. The field should get focus. Scanner: yes. Required fields are shown in text, not only with a red asterisk, and marked with required or aria-required="true". WCAG 3.3.2. Errors are described in text and announced. Say which field is wrong and how to fix it. WCAG 3.3.1, 3.3.3, 4.1.3. Check: submit with a mistake while a screen reader is on. Connect the message to the field with aria-describedby and set aria-invalid="true". Related controls are grouped with <fieldset> and <legend>, for example radio buttons. WCAG 1.3.1. Personal fields use autocomplete (name, email, tel, street-address). WCAG 1.3.5. Check: the browser should offer to fill them. This also helps AI agents fill forms correctly. Don't ask for the same information twice in one process. Pre-fill it or let users select it. WCAG 3.3.7 (new in 2.2). Login doesn't depend on memory or puzzles. Allow paste and password managers. Offer an alternative to cognitive CAPTCHAs. WCAG 3.3.8 (new in 2.2). Changing a field doesn't cause a surprise, such as submitting the form or jumping to another page. WCAG 3.2.2.

Content reflows at 320 CSS pixels wide with no horizontal scrolling (except for content like maps and data tables). WCAG 1.4.10. Check: zoom the browser to 400% on a 1280px-wide window. Touch targets are at least 24×24 CSS pixels, or have enough space around them. WCAG 2.5.8 (new in 2.2). Check: small icon buttons and close (×) buttons are the usual failures. Works in both portrait and landscape. WCAG 1.3.4. Anything done by dragging can also be done with a single click or tap, such as sliders and reordering lists. WCAG 2.5.7 (new in 2.2).

Custom components work with the keyboard and expose the right role and state. Follow the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide pattern for that widget. WCAG 2.1.1, 4.1.2. Check: better still, use the native element (<select>, <dialog>, <details>) and avoid the work. Focus is managed: it moves into a dialog when it opens, stays there, and goes back to the button that opened it. WCAG 2.4.3. Check: the native <dialog> element with showModal() does most of this for you. Content changes are announced with live regions (role="status", role="alert"). The live region must exist in the page before its content changes. WCAG 4.1.3. In single-page apps, route changes are announced: update the <title> and move focus to the new <h1> or announce the new page. WCAG 2.4.2, 2.4.3.

Run an automated scanner in CI (axe-core, pa11y, WAVE, Lighthouse). Treat it as a minimum: it misses most problems that block a whole task. Write end-to-end tests with role-based locators (getByRole), so every test also checks the accessibility tree. Do a keyboard-only check on each changed user flow. Do a screen reader check before each release (NVDA + Firefox, or VoiceOver + Safari). Include people with disabilities in usability testing. Recipes and step-by-step scripts for all of these: Test What Scanners Miss. Sources: WCAG 2.2 · WCAG 2.2 Quick Reference · WebAIM WCAG 2 Checklist · ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

documents.t: Follow WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines): These guidelines provide a framework for making web content more accessible. Use ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) roles and attributes: Enhance screen reader support for dynamic content. Test with screen readers: Tools like NVDA, JAWS, or VoiceOver help simulate the experience of blind users.

Keyboard navigability: Ensure all interactive elements can be accessed without a mouse. Color contrast: Use sufficient contrast between text and background. Responsive design: Make sure content works well on all screen sizes and orientations. Avoid motion triggers: Provide options to reduce motion for users with vestibular disorders.

Automated tools: Use tools like axe, Lighthouse, or WAVE to catch common issues. Manual testing: Combine automated checks with manual testing for a complete picture. Involve users with disabilities: Real user feedback is invaluable.
Use proper tags (<button>, <nav>, <header>, etc.) to give structure and meaning to content. Avoid using <div> and <span> for interactive elements unless enhanced with ARIA.
Choose UI libraries that prioritize accessibility (e.g., Material UI, Reach UI). Contribute accessibility improvements to open-source projects.
Share knowledge with your team and community. Include accessibility in code reviews and development checklists. Advocate for accessibility in product planning and design discussions.

WebAIM: Practical accessibility techniques and tools. W3C WAI: Official accessibility standards and tutorials. Deque University: Training on digital accessibility. MDN Accessibility Docs: Developer-focused documentation.

In the accessibility tree experiment, a registration form that no screen reader user and no AI agent could complete still scored 91/100 in a Lighthouse accessibility audit. This page explains why, and which tests do catch those defects.

Automated scanners such as Lighthouse, axe and WAVE read your markup and check it against rules. They are fast and reliable at what they check. But they can only judge code that tries to be a control: an , an , a
documents.s: Why a high score is not a tested page

documents.t: Layer Tools What it catches Effort 1. Scanner in CI axe-core (Java bindings for Playwright and Selenium), pa11y, IBM Equal Access Checker Missing labels, missing alt text, low contrast, missing landmarks, invalid ARIA Low. Runs on every build. 2. Accessibility tree tests Playwright getByRole and aria snapshots, Testing Library ByRole Controls with no role or no name, fake buttons, fake dropdowns, missing headings Low. Uses tests you already write. 3. Keyboard tests Manual script below, or a scripted Tab path in Playwright Unreachable controls, focus traps, invisible focus, wrong focus order 5 minutes per flow by hand 4. Guided manual check Accessibility Insights for Web (FastPass, Tab stops, Assessment) Issues that need a human: color-only meaning, reading order, meaningful text alternatives 30–60 minutes per page 5. Screen reader check NVDA + Firefox, VoiceOver + Safari Missing or wrong announcements, silent errors, confusing reading order 10 minutes per flow 6. Agent test (optional) An agent limited to accessibility tree tools, like the experiment Whether software acting for a user can finish the task Medium 7. Testing with disabled users Usability sessions with people who use assistive technology every day Real problems that no tool predicts Highest value Layers 1 and 2 belong in CI. Layers 3 and 5 belong in your definition of done for any change to a user flow. Layer 4 fits a release or a quarterly review. Layer 7 is how you find out whether any of it actually works for people.

These are the four defects that broke the registration form in the experiment, plus the general behavior of each kind of test: Defect Scanner (axe / Lighthouse) Tree test (getByRole) Keyboard test Screen reader <span onclick> instead of a link Missed. A span with a click handler has no role to check. Caught. There is no link named "Register". Caught. The span can't get focus. Caught. It's read as plain text, if at all. Placeholder instead of a label Caught (label rule). Not reliable. A placeholder can still be used as the field's name. Missed. The field works with the keyboard. Partly. Some screen readers read the placeholder; it disappears once you type. <div> pretending to be a dropdown Missed. The div has no role. Caught. There is no combobox. Caught. It can't be reached or opened. Caught. It isn't announced as a control. Error shown by color only Missed. Color has no rule to fail. Caught, if you assert a role="alert" message. Missed. Caught. Nothing is read out. The tree test catches three of the four, and it is code you already write. The scanner caught one. That is the difference between "the page passes" and "the task works". If your test can find the control by role and name, so can an agent and a screen reader.

These use Playwright for Java with JUnit 5. Each one fits in an existing end-to-end test. The control names come from a registration form like the one in the experiment; change them to match your own page.

Add the axe-core Playwright bindings (check Maven Central for the latest version): <dependency> <groupId>com.deque.html.axe-core</groupId> <artifactId>playwright</artifactId> <version><!-- latest --></version> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> import com.deque.html.axecore.playwright.AxeBuilder; import com.deque.html.axecore.utilities.axeresults.AxeResults; @Test void registerPageHasNoAxeViolations() { page.navigate(baseUrl + "/register/123"); AxeResults results = new AxeBuilder(page) .withTags(List.of("wcag2a", "wcag2aa", "wcag21a", "wcag21aa", "wcag22aa")) .analyze(); assertTrue(results.getViolations().isEmpty(), () -> results.getViolations().stream() .map(v -> v.getId() + ": " + v.getHelp()) .collect(Collectors.joining("\n"))); } Selenium users can use the com.deque.html.axe-core:selenium artifact, which works the same way with a WebDriver.

@Test void userCanRegisterUsingOnlyRolesAndNames() { page.navigate(baseUrl + "/sessions"); page.getByRole(AriaRole.LINK, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Register")).first().click(); page.getByRole(AriaRole.TEXTBOX, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Full name")).fill("Ada Lovelace"); page.getByRole(AriaRole.TEXTBOX, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Email")).fill("ada@example.com"); page.getByRole(AriaRole.COMBOBOX, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Meal preference")).selectOption("Vegetarian"); page.getByRole(AriaRole.BUTTON, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Register")).click(); assertThat(page.getByRole(AriaRole.MAIN)).containsText("confirmation code"); } Every step fails if the control has no role or no name. On the broken variant, this test fails on the first line.
documents.s: Layer 2: find controls by role and name

documents.t: @Test void invalidEmailErrorIsAnnounced() { page.navigate(baseUrl + "/register/123"); page.getByRole(AriaRole.TEXTBOX, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Email")).fill("not-an-email"); page.getByRole(AriaRole.BUTTON, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Register")).click(); // role="alert" is read out by screen readers as soon as it appears assertThat(page.getByRole(AriaRole.ALERT)).containsText("valid email"); } This is the test that catches "error shown by color only". A red border has no role.
documents.s: Layer 2: check that errors are announced

documents.t: An aria snapshot records the part of the tree you care about, as text. If someone replaces a <select> with a styled <div>, the snapshot no longer matches. @Test void registrationFormTreeIsStable() { page.navigate(baseUrl + "/register/123"); assertThat(page.getByRole(AriaRole.MAIN)).matchesAriaSnapshot(""" - heading "Register" [level=1] - textbox "Full name" - textbox "Email" - combobox "Meal preference" - button "Register" """); } To see what your page looks like today, print it once with System.out.println(page.getByRole(AriaRole.MAIN).ariaSnapshot());. This is the same view the agent in the experiment used to understand the page.

@Test void keyboardUserReachesEveryFieldInOrder() { page.navigate(baseUrl + "/register/123"); List<Locator> expectedOrder = List.of( page.getByRole(AriaRole.TEXTBOX, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Full name")), page.getByRole(AriaRole.TEXTBOX, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Email")), page.getByRole(AriaRole.COMBOBOX, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Meal preference")), page.getByRole(AriaRole.BUTTON, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Register"))); expectedOrder.get(0).focus(); for (int i = 1; i < expectedOrder.size(); i++) { page.keyboard().press("Tab"); assertThat(expectedOrder.get(i)).isFocused(); } } This catches controls that can't get focus and focus that jumps somewhere unexpected. It doesn't check that the focus is visible. That still needs a human, or a visual comparison test.

Java JavaScript / TypeScript com.deque.html.axe-core:playwright @axe-core/playwright page.getByRole(AriaRole.BUTTON, ...) page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Register' }) assertThat(locator).matchesAriaSnapshot(...) await expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot(...) — Testing Library: screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Register' })

Do this by hand for any change to a user flow. Click in the browser's address bar, then press Tab. Focus should land on the first control on the page, or on a "Skip to main content" link. Keep pressing Tab through the whole flow. Write down any control you can't reach. At each stop, check that you can see the focus. A missing outline counts as a failure. Check that the order makes sense: top to bottom, left to right, as the page reads. Use each control: Enter on links and buttons, Space on checkboxes, arrow keys in dropdowns and radio groups, Esc in dialogs. Open any dialog or menu. Check that focus moves into it, stays inside while it's open, and returns to where you were when it closes. Finish the task. If you can't, that's the result of the test.

This uses NVDA on Windows. NVDA works best with Firefox; with some Chromium browsers it may only announce "Chrome legacy window". Install NVDA and start it. Insert is the NVDA key. Ctrl stops speech at any time. Open your page in Firefox. Press Insert+F7 to open the Elements List. Check the Links, Headings, Form fields and Buttons tabs. Every item should have a clear name. "Click here", "button" and blank entries are failures. Press H to jump between headings. The headings should tell you what's on the page without reading it all. Press D to jump between landmarks. You should find at least a main region. Press Tab through the form. Each field should be read with its label, its type and whether it's required. Submit the form with a mistake in it. The error should be read out without you having to look for it. Finish the task with the screen on, then try again with the screen off. On a Mac, VoiceOver (Cmd+F5) with Safari works the same way. Use the Rotor (VO+U) instead of the Elements List.

Write your end-to-end tests with getByRole. It costs nothing extra, and it turns every test into an accessibility tree check. Do the 5-minute keyboard check before you merge any change to a user flow. Then add the scanner to CI, and the screen reader check before each release.

This page follows AI Agents Read Your Accessibility Tree, Not Your HTML. That page showed one flow that worked for nobody but a sighted mouse user. This page shows how to find the same problems in your own app. You don't need a big project to start. Pick one key flow, such as login, checkout or a sign-up form, and do these six steps on it. Steps 1 to 3 take about 20 minutes and need no setup.
documents.s: What to Do Next: Six Steps for Your Own App

documents.t: Open the flow in your browser and inspect it the way an agent or a screen reader does. Chrome or Edge: DevTools → Elements → Accessibility pane. Turn on Enable full-page accessibility tree to see the whole page as a tree. Firefox: DevTools → Accessibility tab. Safari: Web Inspector → Elements → Node sidebar → Accessibility. For every button, link and field, check three things: Property What it is Example Role What kind of control it is button, link, textbox, combobox Name The text a screen reader reads out, and the text an agent searches for "Register", "Email address" State The current condition, if it has one checked, expanded, disabled, invalid A control shown as generic, or with an empty name, is a control that people and agents can't use. If something looks like a button on screen but isn't a button in the tree, it is not a button.
documents.s: 1. Look at your own accessibility tree (5 minutes)

documents.t: Do the same flow with the keyboard only: Key What it should do Tab / Shift+Tab Move to the next / previous control Enter Follow a link, press a button, submit a form Space Press a button, tick a checkbox Arrow keys Move inside dropdowns, radio groups, tabs and menus Esc Close a dialog or a menu Check four things: You can reach every control. You can always see where the focus is. The focus moves in a sensible order. You never get stuck inside a component. If you can't finish the task, neither can a keyboard user, and neither can many agents.

Windows: NVDA (free), with Firefox. Mac: VoiceOver (Cmd+F5), with Safari. Turn off the screen or close your eyes, and try the flow again. Listen for: controls with no name, or a name like "button" or "clickable" form fields read without their label errors that appear on screen but are never read out content read in a confusing order The testing guide has a step-by-step NVDA script.
documents.s: 3. Listen to it with a screen reader (10 minutes)

documents.t: Take one end-to-end test and replace a CSS selector with a role-based locator: // Before: breaks when the markup changes, and proves nothing about accessibility page.locator("div.actions > span:nth-child(2)").click(); // After: fails if the control has no link role or no "Register" name page.getByRole(AriaRole.LINK, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Register")).click(); If your test can't find the control by role and name, an agent can't either. This one change makes your normal tests check the accessibility tree too. It also makes them less brittle, because they no longer depend on the page layout. The same idea works in JavaScript tests with Playwright's page.getByRole() and Testing Library's getByRole.
documents.s: 4. Find one control by role in your tests

documents.t: Add axe-core to your test suite. On every build it catches missing labels, missing alt text, low contrast and missing landmarks. Remember what the experiment showed: the broken form still scored 91/100 in Lighthouse. A scanner can only judge code that tries to be a control. A <div> that pretends to be a dropdown is invisible to it. A passing scan is a minimum, not a result. Test What Scanners Miss explains what each kind of test catches, with copy-paste Java recipes.
documents.s: 5. Keep a scanner in CI, as a minimum

documents.t: Use the Accessible Web Development Checklist. Each item links to its WCAG rule and says how to check it. Look up any rule in the WCAG 2.2 Quick Reference. You can filter it by level (A, AA) and by technology. Before you build a custom widget, read ARIA Roles and check the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide. Stroke Communication Support Guide for Caregivers, for a person who cannot speak, cannot read or write, prefers sound, and can use a touchscreen or gestures. tip Quick note: this is general guidance and not medical advice. For diagnosis or treatment always consult the person’s clinical team (neurologist, Speech-Language Pathologist (SLP), Occupational Therapist (OT), or Physical Therapist (PT)). Caring for someone with aphasia after a stroke can feel overwhelming, but you are not alone. This guide is designed to help you support communication, independence, and emotional well-being for your loved one. We’ve included practical strategies, technology tools, and community resources—all explained in clear, supportive language.
documents.s: Aphasia Communication Quick Start Guide for Caregivers

documents.t: Aphasia is a language disorder caused by brain injury (often stroke) that affects speaking, understanding, reading, or writing. People with aphasia may know what they want to say but struggle to express it or understand others. Other terms you may hear: Apraxia of Speech: Difficulty planning the movements needed for speech. Dysarthria: Slurred or weak speech due to muscle weakness. Aphasia does not affect intelligence. Your loved one is still themselves and can learn new ways to communicate.

Yes/No Gestures: Agree on simple signals (thumbs up/down, head nod/shake, eye movements) for yes/no answers. Practice these together so everyone understands. Use these signals for daily questions: “Are you hungry?” “Do you want to go outside?” Picture Board: Create a laminated board with clear images for basic needs (food, bathroom, pain, help, emotions, family, phone). Pointing to pictures can help express needs when words are hard. You can make your own or use free online templates. Audio Prompts: Record short, familiar questions or statements ("Do you need water?", "Are you comfortable?") on your phone or tablet. Play these as needed to help with routines. Consistent Routines: Use the same signals, prompts, and questions every day. Consistency helps reduce confusion and builds confidence.

These tools can make communication easier. Start with free options and see what works best for your situation. Free Tools: Cboard (Web): Free, picture-based communication app with voice output. Works on computers, tablets, and phones. Google Look to Speak (Android): Select phrases using eye or head movement. Simple and free. Live Transcribe (Android): Real-time speech-to-text for caregivers to show spoken words visually. Google Text-to-Speech / iOS Speak Selection: Built-in voice output for text. Free and easy to set up. Balabolka (Windows): Free text-to-speech program supporting multiple languages. Paid/Commercial Tools: Proloquo2Go (iOS): Robust symbol-based AAC app with voice output. Paid, but highly customizable. Avaz AAC (iOS/Android): Symbol-based communication app. Paid, designed for ease of use. CoughDrop (Web/iOS/Android): Customizable AAC app. Subscription-based, affordable. Voiceitt: Speech recognition for non-standard speech. Paid, innovative for people with unclear speech. Hardware: Tobii Dynavox Eye-Tracking: For those with limited motor control. Clinical-grade, expensive, but life-changing for some. How to choose: Start with free/mobile apps first (Cboard, Google tools) to see what fits your loved one’s needs and abilities. If eye/head control is reliable and mobile/tablet options aren’t enough, ask your clinical team about trying eye-gaze hardware.

Speech-Language Pathologist (SLP): SLPs are experts in communication and can help set up AAC tools, train caregivers, and provide therapy. Occupational Therapist (OT): OTs help adapt devices and routines for daily living. Social Worker: Social workers connect families to emotional support, benefits, and community resources. How to access: Ask your hospital or clinic for referrals. Many services offer teletherapy or home visits.

Online Communities: American Stroke Association Support: Connect with other caregivers and survivors. National Aphasia Association: Practical guides and support groups. Reddit r/stroke: Peer support and tips from other caregivers. Local Support: Ask your hospital’s social worker for local support groups or WhatsApp communities. Rehabilitation centers often offer caregiver support meetings—these are great for sharing experiences and learning from others. Emotional Care: Schedule regular check-ins with family and friends. Even short voice messages or music playlists can lift spirits. If stress or sadness feels overwhelming, ask for a referral to a psychologist or counselor.

Safety: Consider wearable alarms or smart home assistants for emergencies. Medication Reminders: Set up auditory alarms on a phone or smart speaker. Transport & Appointments: Ask your social worker about community transport options for medical visits. Legal & Benefits: Consult local services for disability benefits and caregiver rights.

Asking these questions can help you and your clinical team find the best solutions: What language(s) does your loved one prefer for voice output? Which gestures or movements are most reliable for yes/no? Are there any vision or hearing issues? What are the most important daily needs (food, pain, family contact)? Has your loved one used AAC or speech therapy before? Is there a budget for paid apps or devices? What content does your loved one enjoy (music, family voices, news)?

Set up a tablet with large icons for “Call Family,” “Messages (Voice),” and “Listen” (podcasts or TTS). Install Cboard and Google Look to Speak. Create a laminated picture board and yes/no cards. Place them within easy reach. Record short audio prompts for daily needs and routines. Schedule an SLP evaluation as soon as possible. Keep a daily log of what communication strategies work best.

Supporting a loved one after stroke involves patience, creativity, and knowledge of communication strategies.
Stroke may affect speech, comprehension, memory, and motor skills. Aphasia can make it hard to speak or understand language. Emotional changes like frustration or withdrawal are common.
Use short, clear sentences. Ask yes/no questions when possible. Encourage gestures, drawing, or pointing. Repeat or rephrase if needed—don’t rush.
Try AAC apps like Spoken, Constant Therapy, or Tactus Therapy Use visual aids: photo albums, labeled objects, or printed routines. Create a quiet, distraction-free environment for conversation.
Validate their feelings and celebrate small wins. Join support groups or online communities. Use relaxation tools like Calm to manage stress

Welcome to this accessible and screen reader-friendly guide to understanding the different types of visual impairments. This document is based on reliable medical sources such as the Cleveland Clinic, the American Foundation for the Blind (AFB), and the Center for Parent Information and Resources.
Visual impairment refers to a significant loss of vision that cannot be corrected fully with glasses, contact lenses, medication, or surgery. It includes both partial and complete blindness.

Definition: Partial sight that interferes with daily activities. Characteristics: Difficulty reading, recognizing faces, or seeing in low light. Support: Magnifiers, large print materials, and screen readers.
Definition: Total lack of vision, including the inability to perceive light. Note: This is rare; most people retain some light perception.
Definition: Visual acuity of 20/200 or worse in the better eye with correction, or a visual field of 20 degrees or less. Implication: Qualifies for disability benefits and support services.
Definition: Blindness present at birth. Causes: Genetic conditions, birth defects, or prenatal infections.
Definition: Vision loss due to brain damage, not eye damage. Common in: Children with neurological conditions. Features: Light-gazing, visual latency, and difficulty with visual complexity.
Definition: Difficulty distinguishing certain colors. Types: Red-green, blue-yellow, and total color blindness (achromatopsia). Note: Not a form of blindness but a visual processing difference.
Cause: Vitamin A deficiency. Symptoms: Night blindness, dry eyes, and corneal damage.
Definition: Vision loss due to injury, disease, or aging. Examples: Diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, macular degeneration.
Genetic disorders Infections and trauma Neurological conditions Chronic diseases (e.g., diabetes, hypertension)
Screen readers (e.g., JAWS, NVDA) Braille displays Audio books and tactile graphics AI-powered navigation tools

Accessibility testing checks whether people with disabilities, and the assistive technology they use, can perceive and operate your product. In practice it asks one question: can someone finish the task without a mouse, without sight, without hearing, or with an AI agent acting for them?

Automated tools such as axe, WAVE and Lighthouse check your markup against rules. They are fast and belong in every build. But they only judge code that tries to be a control. A <div> styled as a dropdown has no role, so there is nothing for them to fail. In the accessibility tree experiment, a form that no screen reader user and no AI agent could complete still scored 91/100 in Lighthouse.

ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of HTML attributes that change what the browser puts in the accessibility tree. Screen readers, voice control software and AI agents read that tree to understand the page. They don't read your CSS. A role tells them what an element is: a button, a tab, a dialog, an alert. Together with a name ("Save") and a state (pressed, expanded, checked), it's all they know about a control. See AI Agents Read Your Accessibility Tree for what happens when these are missing.

The first rule of ARIA is: if a native HTML element already does what you need, use it instead of adding a role.
Save
ARIA changes what the element is called, not what it does. role="button" makes a screen reader say "button". It does not make the element focusable, and it does not make Enter or Space work. Every behavior the native element gives you, you have to write and test yourself. That's why WebAIM's yearly scan of the top million home pages keeps finding that pages using ARIA have more detected errors on average, not fewer. Use less of it, but use it correctly.
documents.s: The first rule: use native HTML

documents.t: These native elements already have the right role in the accessibility tree: You write Role in the tree Free behavior <button> button Focus, Enter, Space <a href="..."> link Focus, Enter, listed in "Links" by screen readers <input type="text"> textbox Focus, typing, label connection <input type="checkbox"> checkbox Focus, Space, checked state <select> combobox or listbox Focus, arrow keys, selected state <h1> … <h6> heading (with level) Heading navigation (H key in NVDA) <ul>, <ol> list "List, 5 items" <table> with <th> table, columnheader Table navigation, headers read with each cell <nav>, <main>, <header>, <footer>, <aside> navigation, main, banner, contentinfo, complementary Landmark navigation (D key in NVDA) <dialog> with showModal() dialog Focus moved inside, Esc to close, rest of page blocked <details> / <summary> group / disclosure control Expand and collapse with Enter or Space, expanded state Adding the same role again (<button role="button">, <nav role="navigation">) does nothing. It just adds noise to the code.

Use ARIA when HTML has no element for the pattern, or to expose a state HTML can't express: Need ARIA Notes Tabs role="tablist", role="tab", role="tabpanel", aria-selected Arrow keys move between tabs. See the APG Tabs pattern. Announce a change without moving focus role="status" (polite) or role="alert" (urgent) The element must be in the page before the text changes. A toggle that opens something aria-expanded="true" / "false" on the button, aria-controls Update it every time the state changes. A toggle button aria-pressed="true" / "false" For buttons like "Bold" or a filter. The current page in navigation aria-current="page" Sighted users see it highlighted; this says it out loud. An icon-only button aria-label="Close" Or visually hidden text inside the button. A field with help or error text aria-describedby="id-of-text", aria-invalid="true" The text is read after the label. Hide decoration from screen readers aria-hidden="true" Never on something that can get focus. Before you build any custom widget, look it up in the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG). It lists the roles, states and keyboard behavior each pattern needs, with working examples.

Mistake Why it breaks Fix <div role="button"> without tabindex="0" and key handlers Announced as a button, but keyboard users can't reach or press it Use <button> aria-label on a <div> or <span> with no role Many screen readers ignore names on elements with no role Add a proper role, or use a real control aria-hidden="true" on a focusable element Keyboard focus lands on something the screen reader says doesn't exist Remove it, or also make the element unfocusable (inert, or remove from the Tab order) aria-label that differs from the visible text Voice control users say "click Send", but the control is named "Submit form" Make the name start with the visible text (WCAG 2.5.3) role="presentation" or role="none" on a focusable or interactive element The browser ignores the change, or the control loses its meaning Only use it on purely visual elements, such as layout tables States that are never updated The menu is open, but aria-expanded still says false Update ARIA states in the same code that changes the UI role="menu" for site navigation Screen readers switch to application-menu keyboard mode, which users don't expect on a website Use <nav> with a list of links A live region added to the page at the same time as its message Often nothing is announced Render the empty role="status" element first, then put the text in

Look at the accessibility tree in DevTools (Chrome/Edge: Elements → Accessibility; Firefox: Accessibility tab). Each control should have the role, name and state you expect. Run axe-core. It catches invalid roles, missing required attributes and aria-hidden on focusable elements. It can't tell you whether a role is the right one. Use the keyboard. Every element with an interactive role must work without a mouse. Use role-based locators in your tests, so a missing role fails the build. See Test What Scanners Miss.

Welcome to your guide for starting and advancing your accessibility journey. Whether you're looking for a quick-start plan, formal courses, certifications, or community connections, these resources will help you build and validate your skills. This section is designed to be a living document. If you find a broken link or have a resource to add, please open an issue or submit a pull request!

Use these outlines to focus your learning on the skills most relevant to your role. Designer (2–4 weeks)​ Principles: Master inclusive design, WCAG fundamentals, color contrast, and motion sensitivity. Patterns: Learn to design accessible components (modals, tabs, menus) and define responsive touch targets. Deliverables: Practice creating annotations for focus order, error states, and accessible names. Key Resource: Stark's Library of Accessibility Resources for Designers Front-end Developer (4–6 weeks)​ Fundamentals: Deeply understand semantic HTML, ARIA, and keyboard interaction patterns. Components: Learn to build robust forms, dialogs, and manage focus effectively using the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG). Testing: Integrate automated checks (e.g., axe-core) and practice manual testing with screen readers. Key Resource: MDN Web Docs: Accessibility QA / Tester (2–4 weeks)​ Methodology: Develop test plans covering automated, manual, and assistive technology testing scenarios. Tools: Become proficient with tools like Accessibility Insights for Web and the WAVE Evaluation Tool. Reporting: Learn to file actionable bug reports that include reproduction steps, expected behavior, and relevant WCAG criteria. Key Resource: DHS Trusted Tester Program Product / Leadership (1–2 weeks)​ Strategy: Understand the legal landscape (WCAG, Section 508, EN 301 549) and the business case for accessibility. Governance: Learn how to integrate accessibility into your product lifecycle, from design to release. Metrics: Define and track metrics to measure progress and demonstrate impact. Key Resource: W3C's Business Case for Digital Accessibility

This plan is designed to get you hands-on with core accessibility concepts in one week, using freely available, and wherever possible, open-source tools. Day 1: Foundations & Tools Read: Start with the fundamentals by reading the W3C WAI – Accessibility Fundamentals to understand the scope of web accessibility. Follow this with the Introduction to WCAG to learn about the guidelines that define accessibility. Skim: Get a practical overview with The A11Y Project Checklist. This is a great reference for what to look for. Install Tools: Install browser extensions to help you test. The WAVE extension is a great tool for evaluating web accessibility. Google's Lighthouse is another excellent, open-source tool built directly into Chrome and Edge DevTools. Day 2: Keyboard-Only Navigation Practice: Unplug your mouse and navigate a complex website using only your keyboard. Use Tab to move forward, Shift+Tab to move backward, Enter to activate links and buttons, Space to check/uncheck boxes, and arrow keys for radio buttons and sliders. Learn: Pay close attention to the visible focus indicator (the outline around interactive elements). Is it always visible? Does the order in which you Tab through elements make sense? Read about creating Skip Navigation Links and about The Navigation Section element to allow users to bypass repetitive navigation. Day 3: Semantic HTML and Structure Learn: Dive into the importance of using correct HTML elements for their intended purpose. Use landmarks like <header>, <nav>, <main>, and <footer> to define regions of a page. Ensure headings (<h1> through <h6>) form a logical outline of the content. Read: Get a quick introduction to ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) with ARIA basics in 15 minutes. The first rule of ARIA is to not use ARIA; always prefer using native HTML elements when they are available. Day 4: Images, Media, & Color Contrast Practice: Alternative text is crucial for non-text content. Use the W3C's Alt Text Decision Tree to practice writing meaningful alt text for different types of images (e.g., decorative, functional, complex). Check: Color contrast is vital for readability. Use a Color Contrast Checker to test a site's color palette. Ensure that text and important UI elements meet at least WCAG AA contrast ratios. Day 5: Inclusive Components Learn: Read about a component on Inclusive Components. Choose one that interests you, for example, a "Content Filter" or a "Data Table". Practice: Try to build the component yourself, following the principles from the article. Pay attention to the ARIA attributes and keyboard interactions. Day 6: Automated and Manual Testing Run Automated Checks: Use the tools you installed on Day 1. Run Lighthouse (via the "Audits" or "Lighthouse" panel in your browser's DevTools) and the WAVE extension on a page. These tools can catch many common issues automatically. Practice a Basic Screen Reader Check: Get a feel for how screen readers announce content. Use NVDA on Windows (it's free and open-source) or VoiceOver on macOS (built-in) to navigate and read through a web page. Can you understand the content and operate all controls? Day 7: Review, Fix, and Share Fix: Based on your testing, choose one accessibility issue you discovered this week and fix it in your own code or a demo project. This could be adding a missing label, improving color contrast, or fixing a keyboard navigation trap. Share: Document what you found and how you fixed it. Share this with your team, in a blog post, or on social media. Raising awareness is a key part of building a more accessible web.

A mix of free and paid courses from trusted organizations.

W3Cx on edX: Introduction to Web Accessibility A four-week, self-paced course (4–5 hours/week) with no prerequisites. Created by the W3C WAI and UNESCO, it covers: What accessibility means and who it benefits WCAG 2.1 guidelines and the POUR principles WAI-ARIA for rich internet applications Assistive technology overviews The business case for accessibility Project planning and management strategies Over 88,000 learners have enrolled, and a verified certificate is available for a fee. MDN Web Docs: Accessibility Learning Area An extensive, continually updated hub of tutorials and reference articles. Key topics: Semantic HTML and ARIA roles Keyboard-navigable JavaScript widgets Color contrast, media alternatives, and cognitive accessibility Mobile-first accessibility best practices WCAG compliance steps and how-to guides Each guide includes code examples, checklists, and links to tools. Google Developers: Accessibility Fundamentals A curated set of interactive tutorials and articles on web.dev. Highlights include: “Learn Accessibility” course covering principles and testing workflows Forms accessibility, responsive design, and focus management modules Articles on content patterns, accessible tap targets, and styling focus states Video demos using Chrome DevTools and interviews with accessibility experts Free, self-guided, and ideal for quick reference or deep dives. Udacity: Web Accessibility A free, project-based course taught by industry experts. Through six hands-on lessons—Accessibility Overview, Focus Management, Semantic HTML, Content Navigation, ARIA, and Inclusive Styling—you build real examples and receive mentor feedback. No prior experience required; courses updated as of 2022. Microsoft Learn: Accessibility Fundamentals A learning path (~2 h 40 m) broken into several modules, each module includes interactive labs and knowledge checks. Beginner level, no prerequisites.

Deque University A subscription-based platform with role-specific tracks for developers, designers, testers, and content strategists. Courses range from introductory to advanced testing, policy, and governance. Free access is offered to people with disabilities. Certifications validate skill levels. TPGi ARC Learning Industry-leading accessibility training in both self-paced and instructor-led formats. Topics include WCAG implementation, ARIA design patterns, automated and manual testing methods, accessibility policy, and governance. Delivery options: on-demand modules, live webinars, and on-site workshops. Coursera: University of Illinois – Information Accessibility Design A specialization of five courses covering: Foundations of accessibility theory Web and mobile accessibility techniques Inclusive product design and social media accessibility A capstone project synthesizing learned skills Audit for free or earn a certificate by completing graded assignments. Knowbility Learning Center A Moodle-based platform offering self-paced courses and resources for developers, testers, content authors, educators, and project managers. Key tracks: Accessibility Essentials Accessible WordPress and PDF/Document Accessibility Accessible Information Resource (AIR) competition prep K–12 Access Toolkit and the K12 Access Summit Registration includes both asynchronous modules and live-event sessions through AccessU.

DHS Trusted Tester (TT) Program (US) A free, structured training and certification program for federal employees and contractors. E-learning modules cover web, desktop app, and document testing against Section 508. Certification requires passing a hands-on exam. GOV.UK Service Manual: Accessibility Guidance from the UK Government Digital Service. Explains WCAG success criteria in plain language, illustrated with real-service examples, plus advice on research, procurement, testing, and continuous compliance.

Accessibility is governed by international and regional standards and laws. Key frameworks include: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines): The global standard for web accessibility, developed by the W3C. WCAG Overview ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act): U.S. law prohibiting discrimination based on disability, including digital accessibility. ADA Overview Section 508 (U.S.): Requires federal agencies to make electronic and information technology accessible. Section 508 European Accessibility Act (EAA): EU directive requiring products and services (including digital) to be accessible by 2025. EAA Overview EN 301 549: European standard for ICT accessibility, referenced by the EAA. EN 301 549 How They Relate: WCAG is the technical foundation for most laws and standards worldwide, including ADA, Section 508, and EN 301 549. ADA and Section 508 are U.S.-specific, while EAA and EN 301 549 apply in Europe. The EAA harmonizes accessibility requirements across EU member states, referencing EN 301 549 and WCAG. Compliance with these standards ensures digital products are accessible to people with disabilities and reduces legal risk. Localization & Multilingual Access: Many standards require information to be accessible in multiple languages and formats. This hub aims to provide resources and guidance for global audiences. Further Reading: W3C Accessibility Laws & Policies
